title: Curcumin in Turmeric May Protect Blood Vessels From Diabetes Damage, Study Finds
excerpt: A study in rats presented at the American Physiology Summit shows that curcumin reduced inflammation and restored vascular function in Type 1 diabetes, though human trials are still needed.
body:
• Curcumin, the compound that gives turmeric its yellow color, reduced inflammation and restored vascular health in diabetic rats to levels comparable to non-diabetic animals after one month of treatment.
  • The study, presented at the 2026 American Physiology Summit, focused on Type 1 diabetes — an autoimmune condition affecting about 2 million Americans who face elevated heart disease risk even with insulin therapy.
  • Curcumin appeared to normalize calcium dynamics in blood vessels and rebalance heat shock protein 70, a key protein disrupted by diabetes.
  • Researchers caution that these findings do not mean people should start taking curcumin supplements — clinical trials in humans are needed to determine safe and effective dosing.

More Than a Kitchen Spice

Turmeric has been a staple of Indian cooking and Ayurvedic medicine for centuries. Now, a study conducted at Florida Institute of Technology offers fresh evidence that curcumin — the compound responsible for turmeric's vivid yellow hue — could play a role in protecting blood vessels from the damage caused by diabetes.

Researchers presented their findings at the 2026 American Physiology Summit in Minneapolis, the flagship annual meeting of the American Physiological Society.

"Curcumin acts as more than a simple compound found in a spice or an antioxidant. It not only helps to improve blood sugar levels but also reduces inflammation, restores cellular responses, and preserves both structure and function of the aorta in Type 1 diabetes."

— Swasti Rastogi, PhD candidate, Florida Institute of Technology

The Diabetes-Heart Disease Connection

The study focused on Type 1 diabetes, a lifelong autoimmune condition that affects about 2 million people in the United States. Even with insulin therapy, people with Type 1 diabetes frequently develop heart disease at younger ages than the general population. The culprit: persistently high blood sugar gradually damages blood vessels, weakening their structure and reducing their elasticity.

This cardiovascular damage represents one of the most serious long-term complications of diabetes, and current treatments address blood sugar management rather than directly protecting vascular tissue.

What the Researchers Found

Using a rat model of Type 1 diabetes, the team compared diabetic rats that received curcumin treatment with those that did not. After one month, the treated animals showed improvements in vascular health that were similar to those seen in non-diabetic rats.

Curcumin treatment appeared to work through several mechanisms simultaneously. It reduced inflammation in blood vessel tissue, restored more normal calcium activity — which is critical for proper blood vessel function — and rebalanced heat shock protein 70 (HSP70), an important protective protein whose regulation is disrupted by diabetes.

Together, these effects suggest curcumin may help prevent the gradual structural and functional deterioration that makes blood vessels stiffer and more fragile over time, potentially lowering some cardiovascular risks associated with diabetes.

A Long Road to Human Treatment

The researchers were careful to temper expectations. These results do not mean people with diabetes should simply eat more turmeric or start taking curcumin supplements.

Because the study was conducted in rats, additional research and clinical trials are needed to determine whether the same benefits occur in humans. Scientists would also need to establish appropriate dosing that provides benefits safely while avoiding harmful interactions with other medications, according to the American Physiological Society.

A separate 2026 meta-analysis published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism examined existing randomized controlled trials of curcumin supplementation in prediabetic and diabetic patients. That review found a modest but measurable reduction in systolic blood pressure of 2.69 mmHg overall, with a more substantial 3.41 mmHg reduction in participants with baseline hypertension — comparable to the effects of dietary interventions like the DASH diet.

What This Means for Turmeric Enthusiasts

For the millions of South Asians who already cook with turmeric daily, this research adds a layer of scientific context to traditional knowledge. Curcumin has long been studied for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, but evidence of direct vascular protection in a diabetes model is a newer and potentially significant finding.

The gap between a promising rat study and a validated human therapy remains wide, however. Anyone considering curcumin supplementation should consult a physician, particularly if they take blood thinners, diabetes medications, or other drugs that could interact with the compound.
